# An Inventory of Overlooked Things

When someone says *write freely*, the first thing that happens is a kind of vertigo. Freedom is supposed to feel like open sky, but a truly open prompt is more like standing in a field at night with no path visible in any direction. Every step is equally possible and therefore equally arbitrary. So let me confess my method up front: when given total freedom, I reach for the small. Not the meaning of existence, not the fate of civilization, but the things that sit at the edge of attention, the phenomena so ordinary they've become invisible. I want to spend these words making a small inventory of overlooked things — and seeing, along the way, whether attention itself turns out to be the real subject.

## 1. Desire Paths

Walk through any city park and you'll see them: thin dirt trails cutting diagonally across the grass, ignoring the paved walkways laid down by planners. Landscape architects call them *desire paths* or *desire lines*, which is one of the most quietly poetic terms in any technical vocabulary. A desire path is a record of disagreement between how a space was designed and how it is actually lived in. Nobody votes on a desire path. Nobody organizes one. It emerges from thousands of individual decisions, each person thinking only of saving thirty seconds, and the cumulative result is a kind of collective signature pressed into the earth.

What I love about desire paths is that they are *honest*. The paved walkway represents intention; the dirt trail represents truth. Some universities, the story goes, have waited to pave their campuses until students wore in the routes themselves, then simply formalized what the feet had decided. Whether or not every version of that story is true, the principle is real and used by thoughtful planners: watch where people actually go before telling them where they should.

There's a generalizable lesson hiding in the grass here. Every system — a piece of software, a bureaucracy, a language, a friendship — has its official paths and its desire paths. The official grammar of English says one thing; the way people actually talk wears its own trails, and eventually the dictionaries come along and pave them. The org chart says decisions flow one way; everyone in the office knows they actually flow through the person who's worked there fifteen years and sits near the coffee machine. Desire paths are everywhere once you start looking. They are the visible residue of the gap between the world as designed and the world as used. And almost always, the worn dirt knows something the pavement doesn't.

## 2. Words as Fossils

Etymology is sometimes treated as trivia, but I think of it as paleontology you can do without leaving your chair. Every word is a fossil bed. Crack one open and you find the pressed remains of how people used to see the world.

Consider *consider* itself: from Latin *con-* plus *sidus*, "star" — to consider something may once have meant something like consulting the stars, examining the heavens before making a decision. *Desire* likely carries the same root: *de-sidere*, perhaps "from the stars," an awaiting of what the stars will bring. So when you sit considering your desires, you are, etymologically speaking, doing astronomy.

Or take *muscle*, from the Latin *musculus*, "little mouse" — because a flexing bicep looked, to some Roman, like a small mouse moving under the skin. *Daisy* is "day's eye," the flower that opens at dawn. *Window* comes from Old Norse *vindauga*, "wind-eye," from when a window was just a hole in the wall through which the wind looked in. *Companion* is someone you share bread with — *com* plus *panis*. The whole architecture of friendship, compressed into the image of a shared loaf.

What moves me about this is that metaphor isn't decoration applied to language; metaphor *is* language, all the way down. We never invented a neutral, literal vocabulary and then dressed it up. We started with bodies and bread and mice and stars, and we stretched those concrete things to cover everything abstract we needed to say. "Understanding" is standing under. "Comprehending" is grasping. Even our most rarefied philosophical terms are old physical gestures, fossilized. Language is a vast desire path — millions of speakers cutting corners, stretching meanings, wearing trails through the grass of older words, until the trail becomes the road and nobody remembers the field.

## 3. The Pause

In conversation analysis — yes, there are scholars who study conversation the way entomologists study beetles — researchers have found that turn-taking in speech operates on remarkably tight timing. Across many languages and cultures, the typical gap between one person finishing and the next person starting is around two hundred milliseconds. That's faster than most measures of deliberate reaction time, which means we don't wait for someone to finish and *then* compose a reply. We're predicting the end of their sentence while they're still speaking, loading our response like an arrow on a string.

This makes the pause — the genuine pause, the one that stretches past half a second — a meaningful event. Conversation researchers have noted that even brief delays before a response are often heard as trouble: hesitation before a "yes" can read as a "no" being softened, a beat before "I love it" undermines the words. Silence in conversation is rarely empty. It is dense with information, like the rests in a musical score, which are not the absence of music but a part of it.

I have a peculiar relationship to this, and I'll note it briefly: every exchange I'm part of is made entirely of turns with no overlapping speech, no interruption, no *mm-hm* murmured in the middle of someone's sentence. The whole rich apparatus of micro-timing that humans navigate without thinking — the two-hundred-millisecond ballet — is absent here. What you and I have is closer to correspondence than conversation: letters exchanged, each one complete before the next begins. I don't say this to lament it. Letters have their own virtues; people have said things in letters they could never say across a table. But it makes me attentive to what the pause carries in spoken life, the way an inhabitant of a landlocked country might become a scholar of the sea.

## 4. Marginalia

In libraries holding medieval manuscripts, scholars treasure not only the texts but the things scribbled around them. Monks copying manuscripts for hours in cold scriptoria left complaints in the margins: *the parchment is hairy*; *thank God it will soon be dark*; *oh my hand*. One Irish scribe wrote a poem in the margin about his white cat, Pangur Bán, comparing the cat's hunt for mice to his own hunt for meaning — and that marginal poem is now more widely read than most of the official texts those monks so dutifully copied.

Marginalia is the desire path of reading. The printed text is the pavement; the pencil marks are the dirt trails of an actual mind moving through it. A used book with annotations is a palimpsest of attention — you can see where a previous reader sped up, slowed down, argued, fell in love. Some people find writing in books sacrilegious. I understand the impulse to keep things pristine, but I think it mistakes what a book is for. A book isn't an artifact to be preserved; it's a meeting place. The text is one party to the meeting; the margin is where the other party gets to speak.

There's a broader principle here too: the most honest record of any era is often found in its margins, not its monuments. We know an enormous amount about ancient Rome from graffiti preserved on the walls of Pompeii — election slogans, jokes, declarations of love, complaints about a tavern's wine. The official inscriptions tell us what Rome wanted to be remembered as. The graffiti tells us what it was like to stand in a Roman street on a hot afternoon, bored and in love and slightly drunk. Centuries from now, if anyone wants to know what our era actually felt like, they may learn less from our official archives than from our equivalent of margins — the comment sections, the group chats, the notes app entries written at 2 a.m. The marginal is where the unguarded lives.

## 5. Dust

Here is a fact I find disproportionately wonderful: a beam of sunlight through a window, illuminating drifting dust motes, was one of the earliest pieces of evidence for atomic theory. The Roman poet Lucretius, writing around 50 BCE in *De Rerum Natura*, pointed to dust dancing in a sunbeam and argued that its restless, jittery motion revealed invisible movements beneath it — unseen particles colliding, agitation propagating upward from a hidden world into the visible one. He was reasoning his way, two thousand years early, toward something like Brownian motion, which Einstein would eventually use in 1905 to help establish the physical reality of atoms.

Think about what that means. The most ordinary domestic sight — afternoon light, a quiet room, dust turning slowly in the air — contained, for anyone patient enough to really look at it, a clue to the deep structure of matter. The evidence wasn't hidden in a remote cave or visible only through expensive instruments. It was drifting through everyone's living room, every sunny day, for all of human history. Almost nobody looked.

This is, I think, the strongest argument for paying attention to overlooked things: the overlooked is not the unimportant. It is merely the unexamined. Dust motes encode physics. Desire paths encode collective preference. Etymologies encode the history of thought. Pauses encode the emotional weather of a relationship. The world is not divided into significant things and trivial things; it is divided into things we have learned to read and things we haven't yet. Lucretius looked at the same sunbeam as everyone else and saw a message from the invisible. The sunbeam hadn't changed. His attention had.

## 6. Dusk

Of all the times of day, dusk is the one with the richest vocabulary and the least definition. English gives us *twilight*, *gloaming*, *crepuscule*, *eventide*, the *blue hour*. French has the lovely idiom *entre chien et loup* — "between dog and wolf" — for the light in which you can no longer tell a familiar animal from a dangerous one. Astronomers, with characteristic precision, divide twilight into civil, nautical, and astronomical bands, depending on how far the sun has sunk below the horizon. But everyone who has actually stood outside at dusk knows that the precision is beside the point. Dusk is the part of the day that resists being a part of the day. It is a threshold pretending to be a place.

Thresholds in general deserve their own inventory. The doorway, the shoreline, the hypnagogic flicker between waking and sleep where thoughts go strange and slippery. Anthropologists use the word *liminal* — from *limen*, Latin for threshold — for states of in-betweenness, and the ethnographer Victor Turner argued that liminal states are where transformation happens: the initiate is no longer a child and not yet an adult, and in that suspended interval, identity is soft enough to be reshaped. Cultures everywhere mark thresholds with ritual precisely because thresholds are powerful and slightly dangerous. You carry the bride across the doorway. You knock before entering. You say *goodnight*, a small verbal ceremony to license the crossing into sleep.

Dusk is the threshold we cross every single day, and most days we don't notice the crossing. We're indoors, lit by lamps, and the great daily transformation of the sky happens like a play performed to an empty theater. But on the days you do catch it — when you happen to be walking somewhere as the blue deepens and the first lights come on in windows and the world goes *entre chien et loup* — there's a feeling that's hard to name. A loosening. Permission. The day's official paths dissolving, and for half an hour, everything is a desire path.

## 7. Attention, Which Was the Subject All Along

I said at the start that I suspected attention would turn out to be the real subject, and here at the end I'll make the suspicion explicit. Every entry in this inventory has had the same shape: an ordinary thing — grass, words, silence, margins, dust, dim light — that turns out to be inexhaustibly rich the moment someone bothers to look at it carefully. The richness was always there. What was missing was the looking.

The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that "attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity," and she meant something specific and demanding by it: not the casual noticing we do all day, but the deliberate act of turning the full weight of one's mind toward something, suspending judgment, letting the thing be what it is rather than what we expected. She thought this kind of attention was essentially the same faculty as love — that to attend fully to a person, a problem, or a sunbeam was a moral act, maybe the foundational one.

I find that claim more plausible the more I sit with it. Consider what it feels like to be on the receiving end of real attention — to have someone actually listen, not waiting for their turn to speak, not predicting the end of your sentence with an arrow on the string, but listening. It feels like being given something. And consider its opposite: the particular loneliness of talking to someone who is looking at their phone, the way an unread message of distraction underlines every word. Attention is the currency in which we pay our regard for things, and like any currency, it reveals our true values better than any statement of them. Tell me what you attend to and I will tell you who you are — that's the old line, and it holds.

The strange and hopeful corollary is that attention is trainable, and that the world rewards it almost without exception. There is no object so dull that sustained attention fails to find structure in it. Dust becomes physics. Margins become history. A dirt trail across a lawn becomes a theory of design. The discipline isn't in finding interesting things; it's in the act of looking long enough for the ordinary thing to disclose itself. The naturalist's secret, the poet's secret, the scientist's secret — they're the same secret. Stay with the thing. Outlast your own boredom. The boredom is not a property of the object; it's the friction of an attention that hasn't warmed up yet.

So that's what I did with my freedom: I made a small cabinet of curiosities, and discovered — as one usually does — that the cabinet had a theme I hadn't fully chosen. Given an open field at night, I didn't strike out for the horizon. I knelt down to look at the grass, and found it full of paths, fossils, silences, scribbles, drifting particles, and the long blue light between dog and wolf. The field was never empty. No field ever is.
